rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the eight-compound elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Keep the gradient fixed and raise temperature to test selectivity changes in the central cluster and nearly coeluting final pair. The current short elution window leaves ample room for a shallower gradient later if needed.

Test the low-temperature endpoint with the same gradient to map the alternative selectivity regime. This will show whether cooling separates the central cluster more effectively than heating before refining gradient slope.

Retain the favorable low-temperature selectivity and make the gradient shallower to improve the two remaining critical pairs. The last peak at 6.37 minutes provides room to gain resolution while targeting elution within 10 minutes.

The shallower gradient improved the late pair but drove a central pair toward coelution, indicating a selectivity tradeoff. Raise the starting organic fraction while retaining a relatively shallow slope to test whether that tradeoff can be broken without exceeding 10 minutes.

Test a substantially shallower gradient to see whether the central pair separates again beyond its apparent selectivity crossover. Starting at 0.30 organic should keep the late peaks within a useful time window while the shallow slope improves their resolution.

Keep the shallow gradient that resolves six of seven pairs and test a temperature-induced selectivity shift for the remaining central coelution. A 10-degree increase should reveal whether this pair can separate while preserving the late-pair resolution.

Test a shallower gradient with a lower starting organic fraction to move the central pair beyond its apparent crossover. The low temperature preserves favorable separation elsewhere, while the elevated starting fraction should limit late-peak retention.
Shorten the fully resolving gradient by one grid step to bring the last peak below 10 minutes. The current minimum resolution of 2.30 provides a margin for this modest increase in slope.
The maximum CRF is secured; now test a shorter fully resolved method. Recent slope sensitivity suggests reducing tG to 28 minutes may retain resolution above 1.5 while advancing the last peak.
Shorten the gradient by one more grid step to locate the full-resolution boundary. If the central pair falls below 1.5, injection 10 remains the shortest fully resolved method tested.

Return to the shortest fully resolving gradient and raise temperature by one step to test faster elution. This checks whether the central pair retains sufficient selectivity while the late peaks move earlier.

Test a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower slope to recover central-pair resolution while reducing the initial retention delay. The 0.80 endpoint provides a strong final eluent, and injection 10 remains the fully resolved fallback.

Test whether another temperature step separates the late pair beyond its apparent crossover while preserving central-cluster resolution. This explores a faster selectivity regime, with injection 10 retained as the shortest fully resolved method so far.

Return to the favorable 25 C selectivity and lower the starting organic fraction to test whether the central pair tolerates a steeper gradient. This may produce a shorter fully resolved method than injection 10 while retaining adequate late-pair separation.

Slightly lengthen injection 15's gradient to improve central-pair resolution, while warming to shorten retention. Compared with injection 12, the steeper slope may also separate the final pair more effectively at 30 C.

Return to 25 C and lengthen injection 15's gradient by one step to target its sole unresolved pair. This tests whether the lower starting organic fraction can match full resolution with slightly earlier final elution than injection 10.

With maximum CRF secured, test a higher-organic, faster-eluting regime that may separate the central pair on the opposite side of its crossover. Injection 17 remains the shortest fully resolved fallback.

Shorten the newly successful high-organic gradient while holding its selectivity controls fixed. The minimum resolution of 1.91 offers some margin to advance the final peak while retaining full resolution.
Reduce gradient duration by one grid step to locate the shortest fully resolving slope in this regime. Injection 19 remains the fallback if either critical pair falls below 1.5.

Test a higher starting organic fraction to advance elution, paired with a shallower slope to protect the critical separations. Injection 19 remains the shortest fully resolved method if this changes selectivity unfavorably.

Raise temperature by one step from the shortest fully resolved method to test faster elution and the response of its two critical pairs. Keep injection 19 as the fallback if warming sacrifices full resolution.

Test whether the critical central pair separates again beyond its temperature-driven crossover, potentially yielding a faster fully resolved method. Injection 19 remains the established maximum-score fallback with a 4.14-minute last peak.

Return to the best fast selectivity regime and test a slope between injections 19 and 20 by lowering the endpoint. This checks whether a modestly faster method retains full resolution; injection 19 remains the proven fallback.

Preserve injection 19's successful slope and temperature while ending the programmed gradient much sooner. The gradient endpoint reaches the outlet at 4.65 minutes, after the previously observed 4.14-minute last peak, so full resolution and maximum CRF should be retained.
